items.title: Verizon’s CEO knows Elon Musk is coming for his business. He says it’ll cost SpaceX over $300 billion to compete
items.summary:
Elon Musk wants Starlink to become a major U.S. phone carrier. Verizon CEO Dan Schulman says that if Musk pulls it off, he’ll have spent four to six years and about $300 billion building a copy of Verizon.

“At the end of the day, he might have a network that is pretty much exactly like our network today,” Schulman told Fortune Editor in Chief Alyson Shontell on the latest episode of Fortune ’s Titans and Disruptors of Industry podcast . “There’s no secret sauce, there’s no magic wand, there’s no structural cost advantage that will come out. He’ll have a network, and in four years, five, six years, he’ll be the sixth entrant into the market.”

Musk added to that picture Wednesday, telling the New York Times DealBook Summit that SpaceX is looking into the production of “micro cell towers” for Starlink Mobile as early as next year, referring to ground hardware that Schulman says turns SpaceX into just another carrier.

Last month, Elon Musk’s SpaceX announced plans for satellite internet service Starlink to become “a major mobile carrier in the U.S.,” sending telecom stocks plunging and market caps for the three major U.S. carriers sliding by $50 billion. Verizon alone dropped 8.7%, marking its worst single-day performance since 2002.

SpaceX acquired wireless spectrum from telecommunications company Echostar in a $17 billion deal in September 2025, which, following Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approval in May, laid the groundwork for the company to launch the Starlink Mobile, which would differ from other carriers by not requiring a dish or router, but by…
items.t: Verizon’s CEO knows Elon Musk is coming for his business. He says it’ll cost SpaceX over $300 billion to compete

items.title: Crypto platform’s plan to offer tokenized shares for Anthropic IPO comes up short, following similar SpaceX flop
items.summary:
In the lead up to Anthropic’s record-setting Thursday IPO , several crypto platforms announced plans to offer their customers exposure to the offering in the form of tokens tied to its shares. It’s far from clear, however, whether these tokenized stocks—crypto tokens designed to track a stock’s price—will actually provide exposure at Anthropic’s offering price, or at all. The maker of the Claude chatbot opened at $111.50 a share on Nasdaq, about 34% above its $83 IPO price. 

Binance Wallet, the wallet tied to the crypto exchange, is already off to a rocky start. Minutes after the stock began trading, the platform said it hadn’t secured enough shares to fill customers’ orders. It said it would refund everyone who put up money and split the available tokens among eligible customers for free, based on how much each had committed. 

The announcement came a day after Binanced Wallet opened Anthropic-linked tokens at the company’s eventual IPO price, plus a 5% fee. Within hours, users had committed $500 million, hitting the campaign’s cap and prompting it to close early. Firms like Binance typically offer tokenized stocks by obtaining allocations of shares for themselves, which they hold in custody, and then issue tokens that serve as claims on the stock.

Kraken also let eligible customers request Anthropic-linked tokens at the final IPO price plus 5%, without guaranteeing an allocation. Ondo, a tokenization platform, took a different approach. It said it would launch its token once Anthropic shares began trading on Nasdaq, giving buyers exposure at market prices rather than a…
items.t: Crypto platform’s plan to offer tokenized shares for Anthropic IPO comes up short, following similar SpaceX flop

items.title: Thanksgiving dinner for 10 costs $78.93 this year — about 25% more than before the pandemic, with fresh turkey up 11%
items.summary:
Inflation-weary Americans have at least some good news to cheer this holiday season: The cost of a basic Thanksgiving meal has stabilized.

A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people clocks in at $78.93, approximately 0.4% less than in 2025, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute . That’s because most staples haven’t seen a sharp jump in prices.

Americans are still justified in feeling stressed about high grocery bills, but it’s because of the cumulative effect of rising prices in recent years. While inflation has slowed since its peak of more than 9% in 2022 , the cost of a Thanksgiving meal is roughly 25% higher than it was before the COVID-19 pandemic began .

I’m an agricultural economist who has been studying the many drivers of food inflation. What’s key to remember is that inflation data tells us how quickly prices are increasing, not whether prices are returning to previous levels. So even modest price jumps today are layered on already-elevated prices.

Here’s what Americans can expect when they go shopping for Thanksgiving, from turkey to dessert:

Go for frozen turkey 

Stable frozen turkey prices have played an important role in keeping overall holiday meal costs close to last year’s levels.

The average advertised price for a frozen turkey over 16 pounds (about 7 kilograms) was $0.96 per pound, essentially unchanged from the $0.97 per pound in the same period last year, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Turkey Report , published on Nov. 13, 2026. These prices reflect the typical discounts leading up to Thanksgiving, when…
items.t: Thanksgiving dinner for 10 costs $78.93 this year — about 25% more than before the pandemic, with fresh turkey up 11%

items.title: Microsoft’s Outlook outage didn’t end when it was fixed — a backlog of retried emails can take hours to days to clear
items.summary:
The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service.

Microsoft reported on Nov. 13 that the company is “continuing to see improvements in service availability” but that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery.”

Despite decades of predictions about its decline , email remains a central pillar of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage affected businesses, governments and schools around the world.

When most people think about cloud outages , they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service.

Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn’t designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises.

Old architecture 

When a typical cloud service breaks , it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers…
items.t: Microsoft’s Outlook outage didn’t end when it was fixed — a backlog of retried emails can take hours to days to clear

items.title: Elon Musk went from ‘dark MAGA’ to ‘not MAGA’ after spending $445 million on a Republican midterm defeat
items.summary:
Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars trying to fill the halls of Congress with Republicans, watched them lose anyway, and now says he’s not even sure what MAGA means.

The world’s richest man, who once proudly declared himself “dark MAGA,” appeared to have a change of heart Wednesday at The New York Times DealBook Summit, where he told Andrew Ross Sorkin he doesn’t consider himself part of the movement he spent years championing.

“I’m not MAGA,” Musk said, before quickly qualifying his statement. “Well, at least I’m not like, I’m not sure what MAGA means.”

The apparent shift came just weeks after Musk poured more than $445 million into Republican candidates and political groups during the 2026 election cycle, only to watch Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress . And for once, the world’s richest man seemed to have some buyer’s remorse.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk said. “Or maybe it would have been much worse without that.”

His spending had made him one of the most influential donors in American politics, but it hadn’t delivered the Republican majority he wanted. “It certainly shows that American elections are not just about money,” he said. “Probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

With Democrats taking control of Congress, Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming House Oversight Committee chair, has signaled plans to scrutinize Musk’s businesses and his role in DOGE and the firing of federal workers.

It’s quite a different tune from October 2024, when Musk…
items.t: Elon Musk went from ‘dark MAGA’ to ‘not MAGA’ after spending $445 million on a Republican midterm defeat

items.title: Want to build an AI operating model? First, build consensus
items.summary:
At a recent dinner with chief operating officers in New York City, we caught up with the senior leaders most often tasked with transforming AI use into value. The conversation was markedly different from the ones we were having just one year ago.

In 2025, peers in the C-suite would boast about individual AI successes: An agent that made software engineers more productive, or an AI use case in accounting that dethroned the spreadsheet.

But this year, conversations were focused on the forest, not the trees. Individual successes felt insufficient. The bigger question was: How do you do this again and again? How do you build a foundation that makes AI success second nature ?

Leaders want an AI Operating Model: an enterprise-wide foundation that makes agents, automation, and intelligent data routine. Because the alternative is exhausting: fighting tooth and nail to scale individual AI projects.

Unfortunately, exhaustion is the status quo.

Why? One reason is a misconception about who builds the AI Operating Model. Ask who owns AI, and every executive raises a hand: the CIO for the technology, the CAIO for the models, the CFO for the investment, the CHRO for the workforce.

In reality, it’s a joint effort across the C-suite. Still, someone must steward these efforts. Often that’s the COO, whose remit spans every function. But even the COO can’t make executive decisions across every business unit. Instead, they need to build consensus. And so a decidedly old-school skill – influence – is at the center of AI success today. Rolling up your sleeves and building relationships,…
items.t: Want to build an AI operating model? First, build consensus

items.title: Anthropic stock pops 30% to $2 trillion market cap in mega IPO
items.summary:
Anthropic’s stock surged more than 30% in first minutes as a public company, a roaring debut that crowned the AI company—at least briefly—with a stunning, $2 trillion market cap.

Shares of Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share on Thursday, up 34% from the $83 IPO price. The stock pop began to moderate somewhat as the trading day continued, with shares trading up 14%, at $94.50 per share.

Shares of Anthropic, under the ticker symbol “ANT,” began trading a couple of hours after the stock market’s opening bell. The strong demand for Anthropic shares came as the broader market was under pressure, with the Nasdaq down 363 points and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 1038 points in midday trading.

At the $111.50 opening price, Anthropic’s market cap was roughly $2 trillion—an astounding Wall Street debut that instantly puts the five-year-old AI company in the elite club of trillion-dollar public companies.

“This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in a statemen t posted on X on Thursday.

Anthropic priced the offering Wednesday night at $83 a share , above its marketed range of $70 to $78, giving the company a $1.5 trillion valuation. Demand was strong enough that it raised the deal to 980 million shares from 825 million.

There had been endless speculation about whether Anthropic would top SpaceX as the largest IPO of all time. At a $1.5 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would be the second most…

items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.summary:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org
items.t: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras

items.title: iPhone designer Tony Fadell’s next big thing: Bringing AI to fashion in hopes of saving H&M $100 million a year
items.summary:
The fashion business thrives on the conceit that it is modern, on-trend, and all about what’s happening right now . But behind the scenes—in the textile mills and garment factories that supply major brands—is an industry that runs much as it did in the 1970s. Its supply chains are splintered, chaotic, and based in warehouses that are so old-fashioned they may not even be on the internet, according to Max Easton, CEO of Smartex.AI.

Most of the work is done by hand. Checking the quality of the fabric, for instance, will be performed by a worker holding a handful of color swatches, watching a roll of cloth go by all day.

“They’re looking for simple physical defects like holes, needles, the wrong yarn, something that would be noticeable in a garment, right?” Easton said to Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon this year. For most brands, there is no such thing as a “white” T-shirt. It needs to be exactly the right shade of white—which might be a brilliant white or a creamier off-white.

But because the work is inspected by humans, fashion brands can never be quite sure that the quality of the fabric they’re buying is going to be consistent, or even match what they ordered.

“If you go to any kind of [fashion] supply chain, whether it’s fabric production or garment production, most people are just kind of amazed by how chaotic it is,” Easton said.

The chaos ends now, Smartex hopes. 

The company has been working with Tony Fadell, the legendary codesigner of the iPod, iPhone, and Nest doorbell, to launch a physical AI product that can perform fabric quality checks continuously, at…
items.t: iPhone designer Tony Fadell’s next big thing: Bringing AI to fashion in hopes of saving H&M $100 million a year

The actor’s latest roles see him go from a delivery guy on £40 a day to the notorious crypto scammer who stole more than $10bn. His sympathies are clear: ‘I wasn’t brought up to care about money,’ he says

In the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief Is the Thing with Feathers at St Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn. Afterwards, the 24-year-old actor hung around the stage door. “There were 500 people queueing up for Cillian, but I was the only one who wanted to meet Enda Walsh,” says Boyle, laughing. When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’”

Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. Then, a few years later, he received a letter from Walsh explaining that he was adapting Keiran Goddard’s 2024 novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, about five close friends from a council estate in Birmingham who find themselves questioning everything about their precarious lives as they hit 30. He had scripted the part of Patrick, a politically outspoken graduate working as a zero-hours…
items.t: ‘Sam-Bankman Fried messaged me from prison’: rising star Anthony Boyle on playing the disgraced tech bro – and a zero-hours bike courier

items.title: I tested an AI startup that claimed it could beat Wall Street earnings estimates. It won 40 out of 50 times
items.summary:
In 1997, a Fortune journalist observed , “The simplest, most visible, most merciless measure of corporate success … has become this one: Did you make your earnings last quarter?” Those words hold up just as well today. Indeed, the current Q3 earnings season has featured the same, decades-old ritual: Investors wait to discover if a firm can meet or exceed a consensus target from Wall Street analysts—and then reward or punish the company’s share price accordingly. Now, that ritual could be in for a shake-up.

In October, I was approached by a financial AI startup called Samaya that claimed it could predict earnings outcomes more accurately than the analysts. Prove it, I said. I invited Samaya, which raised $43 million from prominent investors in 2025, to put its money where its mouth is and provide Q3 predictions for 50 big companies, ranging from Coca-Cola to Carvana , prior to their earnings releases.

The company accepted the challenge. This led to a two-week experiment in which we placed Samaya’s AI predictions alongside the consensus view of Wall Street analysts in a spreadsheet, and then recorded the actual Q3 earnings number. Samaya didn’t just beat the analysts, it smoked them. For 40 out of the 50 companies, the AI startup’s forecasts were more accurate than the Wall Street consensus and, in most of these cases, by a considerable margin.

The experiment represents a small sample over a single earnings period, but it has potentially large implications for investors, companies, and analysts alike. More broadly, the exercise underscored, once again, how AI is…
items.t: I tested an AI startup that claimed it could beat Wall Street earnings estimates. It won 40 out of 50 times

items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...

items.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
items.summary:
It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year

  • Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166

The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January. But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving.

Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use.

Continue reading...
items.t: Energy price cap rise: how to beat the January hike

items.title: David Beckham's perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary:
The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares

Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while, and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down.

Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire. I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company, Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m).

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

items.title: Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth
items.summary:
Every CEO I talk to has an AI savings plan. Almost none have an AI revenue plan.

Savings matter. But an AI strategy that stops there is incomplete.

Across 50 years of entrepreneurship, I’ve helped create more than 175 companies. I’ve watched successive technology waves play out the same way. The first instinct is to use the new tool to do the old things cheaper. The companies that win use it to do new things. Electricity didn’t just lower factory power bills; it let factories be rebuilt around the assembly line. The internet didn’t just cut the cost of mailing catalogs; it created Amazon .

An EY-Parthenon survey published in April 2026 found that 63% of growth leaders at large U.S. companies said their organizations were using AI primarily for efficiency and productivity. Just 7% cited diversifying revenue streams. McKinsey’s 2026 research finds that AI high performers pursue growth or innovation alongside efficiency.

In a 2025 study of software and reasoning tasks, METR found that the length of tasks AI agents could complete with 50% reliability had been doubling roughly every seven months. Those lengths reflect how long the tasks take human experts.

AI is making ideas more abundant and early experimentation less expensive. For software-based concepts, it can help teams research a market, write and test code, and build an initial prototype before committing a larger team and budget. The hard part remains choosing the right opportunities, validating demand, and turning them into viable businesses. Established companies can draw on existing expertise and capabilities…
items.t: Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth
